front: [Chain: REPO 1/4] A dealer funds a £50m gilt position through a classic repo at 4.00% for 14 days. Describe the cash flows of the repo and compute the interest.
back:
Headline: a repo is a sale of securities for cash with an agreed repurchase at a later date at a higher price. The cash borrower is the collateral seller; the cash lender is the collateral buyer (reverse-repo side).
Repurchase price: \(P_{rep}=P_0\left(1+r\,\dfrac{d}{B}\right)\), with \(B=365\) for GBP and \(B=360\) for USD and EUR.
Interest: \(50{,}000{,}000\times 0.04\times \dfrac{14}{365}=£76{,}712\), so the repurchase price is £50,076,712.
Coupons on the collateral during the term flow to the economic owner (the cash borrower) under GMRA or GMSLA conventions, so the repo rate is purely a financing rate and is separate from the collateral's yield.
Interviewer follow-up: why does the lender not earn the bond coupon? Because the lender holds title only as security; coupons are passed back to the seller, so the lender's P&L is the repo interest plus any haircut or margin.
Classic repo over 14 days: cash and gilt legs, repurchase price GBP 50,076,712.

front: [Chain: REPO 2/4] Same £50m repo, but the cash lender takes gilts with a 5% haircut. What collateral market value is needed, and what risk does the haircut cover?
back:
Headline: market value of collateral \(=50/(1-0.05)=£52.63\text{m}\). Cash lent = MV \(\times(1-h)\).
The haircut protects the lender against a fall in collateral value between the last margin call and the completed liquidation (the margin period of risk, typically a few days for gilts). A rough sizing is \(h \approx \sigma\sqrt{\tau_{liq}}\times z\) plus liquidity and concentration add-ons; the number is an approximation, not a derivation.
Haircuts are lower for short-dated, liquid government collateral and higher for long-dated bonds, equities and credit.
Interviewer follow-up: why are haircuts procyclical? Haircut models are volatility-based, so they rise after a volatility spike, which cuts cash available against the same bonds at the moment funding is scarcest (see the stress case in this set).

front: [Chain: REPO 3/4] The same gilt repo can settle bilaterally on a DVP basis, through a tri-party agent, or through a CCP. What differs in collateral control, intraday risk and netting?
back:
Tri-party: a clearing bank (tri-party agent) holds the collateral, runs allocation, substitution and daily margin, and typically extends intraday credit to the cash borrower before end-of-day unwind.
Bilateral DVP: each leg settles against payment through a settlement system, with gross settlement and no tri-party intraday credit, but no multilateral netting.
CCP-cleared repo (e.g. LCH RepoClear in Europe, FICC in the US, approx.): the CCP novates both sides and nets positions multilaterally, which reduces gross exposure and the number of settlements.
Interviewer follow-up: why does a dealer still hold gross repo on balance sheet even if it nets at a CCP? Accounting netting is narrower than economic netting (see the netting card in the balance-sheet chain).

front: [Chain: REPO 4/4] A dealer funds £100m of gilts at a 2% haircut with £2m of equity. In a volatility spike the haircut is raised to 10% and equity is fixed at £2m. What is the funding consequence and why is it procyclical?
back:
Headline: at 10% the maximum position supportable by £2m of equity is \(2/0.10=£20\text{m}\), so the desk must sell about £80m of gilts.
At 2%: cash \(=98\), equity \(=2\), position \(=100\). At 10%: cash \(=90\), so to keep £100m of bonds the desk needs £10m of equity, an £8m shortfall.
Procyclicality: the haircut rises when volatility rises, forced sales push prices down and volatility up, and the loop repeats. This is the same mechanism that drove the 2022 UK LDI episode (spread pressure on leveraged funds with collateral calls).
Interviewer follow-up: what can a dealer do to limit the loop? Pre-fund margin, hold a liquidity buffer of unencumbered HQLA, term out funding and negotiate haircut floors.
Haircut 2% to 10% on GBP 100m with GBP 2m equity: cash falls, GBP 8m equity shortfall.

front: [Chain: SPEC 1/4] A gilt is special in repo at 3.20% against 4.00% general collateral (GC). Who benefits from specialness, and what does the short seller give up?
back:
Headline: specialness is the spread GC minus special rate = 80bp. Value goes to whoever needs the specific bond.
The holder who repos the bond out (cash borrower) pays 3.20% instead of 4.00%, so the bond holder gets cheaper funding.
The short seller borrows the bond by lending cash through reverse repo at 3.20%, forgoing 80bp on the cash.
Value of specialness to the holder: £10m for 30 days gives \(10{,}000{,}000\times 0.008\times 30/365=£6{,}575\).
Interviewer follow-up: why does a dealer accept the cost? It is cheaper than a fail, which carries a penalty and a failure to hedge, and is cheaper than paying the market for a bond it cannot source.

front: [Chain: SPEC 2/4] A short seller fails to deliver a special bond on settlement date. What does the buyer receive, and how is the fails charge set?
back:
Headline: the buyer keeps its cash and receives a fails charge that compensates it for the lost use of cash.
Market practice (US TMPG fails charge, approx.): the charge rate is \(\max(3\%-r_{ref},\,0)\) per annum, where \(r_{ref}\) is the TMPG reference rate (the fed funds target, or the lower bound of the target range). The charge is \(C=P\times\max(3\%-r_{ref},0)\times d/360\) for \(d\) days of fail, paid by the failing seller.
Example: a $100m fail for 2 days at a 1.50% reference rate gives a 1.50% charge, so \(100\text{m}\times 0.015\times 2/360=\$8{,}333\).
Where it breaks: at a reference rate of 3% or more the charge is zero, so a fail carries no direct fee in a higher-rate regime. The charge rises as the reference rate falls, so fails are costlier when rates are low. The formula is specific to the TMPG framework and was revised over time (approx.; verify the current TMPG document).
Interviewer follow-up: why would a desk prefer to fail rather than borrow? When the charge is zero or small and the bond is expensive to borrow, failing can be cheaper than paying a high special rate, although the buyer's lost hedge and carry still sit with the market.

front: [Chain: SPEC 3/4] Specialness deepens until a 1-day repo on €100m of a bond prints at -0.50% (Act/360). Show the repurchase price and explain why the cash lender accepts paying.
back:
Headline: the cash lender pays rather than earns. Repurchase price \(=100\text{m}\left(1-\dfrac{0.005}{360}\right)=€99{,}998{,}611\), so the lender pays €1,389 for one day, or €13,889 for 10 days.
The lender accepts because it needs the specific bond (to deliver, hedge, or avoid a fail). Its alternative is depositing cash with the central bank.
Negative repo is bounded below by the deposit alternative: if the central bank deposit rate is itself negative (euro area 2014 to 2022 and similar regimes, approx.), negative GC and special rates can extend below zero, but the depth is limited by the cost of cash deposits and by whether the deposit rate is tiered.
Interviewer follow-up: does a negative repo rate give a bond holder a free lunch? Yes, a negative special lets the holder be paid to lend cash to it, which is why negative specials persist only while the bond is scarce.

front: [Chain: SPEC 4/4] The cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) bond in a government bond future trades special in repo at 3.20% while the market prices the futures off an implied repo of 4.30%. What is the excess carry and how does specialness feed into the cash-futures basis?
back:
Headline: the excess carry for a long CTD position financed at 3.20% against an implied repo of 4.30% is 110bp per annum. Per 100 of dirty price over 90 days: \(100\times 0.011\times 90/360=0.275\).
Mechanism: the implied repo is the rate at which buy-the-bond-and-deliver is riskless. If the CTD's actual financing is special, the realized carry of holding it exceeds the implied-repo benchmark. A basis trader buys the CTD, shorts the future and collects the difference.
Where it breaks: CTD specialness is transient and the CTD can switch when relative specialness changes (the switch option), so the basis trade carries the risk that the CTD changes or that specialness disappears.
Interviewer follow-up: how does this link to the specialness of the CTD being priced into the futures? Specialness lowers the effective cost of carrying the CTD, which is why the futures price and the CTD's net basis move together.

front: [Chain: SONIA 1/4] Sterling overnight money markets: how is reformed SONIA formed, published and accrued?
back:
Headline: SONIA is the Bank of England's published overnight rate for unsecured sterling wholesale deposits, based on transaction data for the previous business day.
Reformed SONIA (since April 2018, approx.) is a volume-weighted trimmed mean of the transaction rates in the middle of the volume distribution (the central 50% of the volume distribution, per the Bank of England), which reduces the influence of outliers and thin trades.
Accrual is Act/365 Fixed, compounded in arrears for loans and swaps (daily compounding over the period, with a lookback or observation shift depending on the product).
Where it breaks: the rate rests on a transaction base that can thin out in stress, so the unsecured series can diverge from the secured repo rate (the SONIA-repo basis).
Interviewer follow-up: why is SONIA unsecured while the desk's funding is secured? Because the reference rate is for wholesale unsecured cash; secured funding is priced off repo, and the difference is the secured-unsecured basis.

front: [Chain: SONIA 2/4] Under the Bank of England's floor system, why does SONIA sit close to Bank Rate, and why can it trade a few basis points below it?
back:
Headline: in a floor system the central bank pays Bank Rate on reserves, so a bank with reserves will not lend overnight in the interbank market below Bank Rate. Market rates are therefore anchored near Bank Rate.
SONIA can print below Bank Rate because non-bank lenders such as money market funds have no access to reserve remuneration and will accept less than Bank Rate from banks, which are able to earn Bank Rate on their reserves. The gap is a few basis points (approx.) and reflects who can access the facility.
Where it breaks: the anchor is the rate paid on reserves, not Bank Rate per se. If the reserve remuneration rate is set below Bank Rate (a technical rate), the floor moves.
Interviewer follow-up: what happens to SONIA when reserves fall? It moves up toward the reserve-scarcity region, as the next card covers.

front: [Chain: SONIA 3/4] Quantitative tightening drains central bank reserves. Describe the reserve demand curve and why repo and SONIA can jump above Bank Rate before reserves are fully exhausted.
back:
Headline: the demand for reserves is flat at high reserve levels (any surplus is remunerated at the floor), then steepens sharply as reserves approach the level banks need for intraday payments, liquidity rules and internal limits. The curve is convex.
So a moderate QT drain from ample reserves costs almost nothing, but a drain near the kink produces a spike in overnight repo and SONIA above Bank Rate.
Why the spike comes earlier than aggregate scarcity: reserves are unevenly distributed. A few large banks can be short even when the aggregate is adequate, and tax dates or large Treasury or gilt settlements can drain the marginal bank at a point in time.
Interviewer follow-up: how would you measure distance to the kink? Use the spread of overnight repo or SONIA over Bank Rate, intraday reserve usage and the distribution of reserves across banks, not the aggregate level alone.

front: [Chain: SONIA 4/4] Why does the Bank of England maintain standing and term liquidity facilities alongside its reserve regime? Give the function of the standing facility, the indexed term repo, and the contingent term repo facility.
back:
Headline: the framework separates the policy rate from the liquidity tools that stop repo and SONIA from spiking.
Standing facility (Standing Lending Facility): overnight lending against eligible collateral at a penal rate above Bank Rate, which caps the marginal cost of overnight liquidity for banks that have collateral.
Short-Term Repo (STR): announced 4 August 2022. It supplies reserves at Bank Rate for a 7-day term against Level A collateral, in unlimited amounts, to keep short-term market rates near Bank Rate as central bank reserves fell during gilt sales.
Indexed Long-Term Repo (ILTR): term funding against a broad collateral set, priced to be neutral to the policy stance. The facility predates 2022 in its current form, so its launch date is not stated here (unverified).
Contingent Term Repo Facility (CTRF): a liquidity insurance facility that lends reserves for three months against less liquid collateral. It is designed to be activated in stress rather than run in normal times. Its launch date is unverified (sources differ).
Caveat: rates, eligible collateral and launch details have changed over time. Verify the current BoE framework before quoting numbers.
Interviewer follow-up: how does a standing facility interact with a floor system? A penal standing rate sits above Bank Rate, so the facility limits upward spikes while the reserve remuneration rate sets the floor.

front: [Chain: SOFR 1/4] SOFR is the USD risk-free rate. What is its transaction base, and why does the market build term SOFR separately?
back:
Headline: SOFR is a volume-weighted median of overnight Treasury repo transactions, drawn from tri-party repo, General Collateral Finance (GCF) and bilateral DVP. The New York Fed publishes it the morning after.
Because it is secured and overnight it has no term or bank-credit component, so it is not a term rate. Term SOFR is derived from futures and swap markets rather than from transactions, and most swaps and loans compound overnight SOFR in arrears instead.
Where it breaks: when repo volume is concentrated in a few trades or specific collateral, the median can move on thin flows, so the fixing reflects the repo market's structure, not its average.
Interviewer follow-up: why could SOFR print above the interest on reserves rate? Because reserve scarcity pushes the marginal repo borrower to pay above the reserve remuneration rate, which is the same mechanism as the SONIA reserve-demand kink.

front: [Chain: SOFR 2/4] On 17 September 2019 overnight repo spiked. What was the mechanism, and what were the approximate sizes of the move?
back:
Headline: SOFR printed about 5.25% that day, with intraday trades reportedly near 10% (approx. figures; verify before quoting), from about 2.43% on 16 September (approx.; verify before quoting).
Mechanism: reserves had been drained by a combination of a corporate tax date, Treasury settlements and a fall in aggregate reserves. The marginal bank with a reserve shortfall was forced to borrow in repo, and balance-sheet and regulatory constraints limited intermediation, so the spike was not arbitraged away.
Response: the Fed injected overnight repo liquidity and later built standing facilities to stop a repeat.
Interviewer follow-up: what is the lesson for scenario analysis? Aggregate reserves are not sufficient. Model the distribution of reserves, the calendar of tax and settlement flows, and the constraints that stop intermediaries from using their balance sheet.

front: [Chain: SOFR 3/4] How do the Fed's overnight reverse repo (ON RRP) facility and its Standing Repo Facility (SRF) bound SOFR, and where do they sit in the target range?
back:
Headline: the ON RRP rate sits at the bottom of the target range and gives eligible money-market funds a floor for lending cash. The SRF rate sits at the top of the range and gives dealers with eligible Treasury collateral a ceiling for borrowing cash.
The interest on reserves rate sits inside the range. In the ample-reserve regime SOFR tends to trade near the RRP floor; as reserves become scarce, it moves up toward IORB and, in stress, toward the SRF rate.
The Fed established the standing repo facility on 28 July 2021. The overnight repo operations run from September 2019 preceded it (approx.).
Interviewer follow-up: why would a dealer ever pay the SRF rate when it can borrow in the market? Only when the market rate is above the SRF rate, which is the stress condition the facility exists to cap.

front: [Chain: SOFR 4/4] The SEC's 2023 rule requires central clearing of eligible US Treasury cash and repo transactions. What is the rationale, what are the approximate compliance dates, and what role does sponsored repo play?
back:
Headline: the rule aims to reduce counterparty risk and improve resilience by pushing eligible Treasury trades through a covered clearing agency, principally FICC.
Compliance dates (per the SEC February 2025 extension, checked against press coverage; no later change found): the original timeline was December 2025 for cash and June 2026 for repo. In early 2025 the SEC extended both by one year, to December 2026 for cash and June 2027 for repo.
Sponsored repo: a sponsoring member submits client trades to FICC, so non-dealer clients such as funds can access FICC netting. The sponsor takes on the client's clearing exposure and the associated balance-sheet and margin cost.
Where it breaks: sponsored clients get netting only through the sponsor's membership, so access and concentration of sponsors become the key operational risks.
Interviewer follow-up: why does clearing change balance-sheet cost? Netting at a CCP reduces gross exposure and can lower leverage-based charges, which is why dealers' funding economics shift after the mandate.

front: Derivation: Convert a repo rate quoted on Act/360 into the equivalent Act/365 rate. Give the step-by-step and the numerical result for 4.00% Act/360.
back:
Step 1: the interest on principal \(P\) for \(d\) days is \(I=P\,r_{360}\,d/360\) under Act/360 and \(I=P\,r_{365}\,d/365\) under Act/365.
Step 2: equate the two to get the same money: \(r_{360}/360 = r_{365}/365\), so \(r_{365}=r_{360}\cdot 365/360\).
Step 3: plug in 4.00%: \(r_{365}=4.00\%\times 365/360=4.056\%\), about 4.06%.
Where it breaks: the relation holds only for simple interest over one period. For compounded rates the basis change is applied to the periodic rate, and mixed-basis curves need the conversion applied consistently to both legs of a basis swap.

front: Derivation: Two term repo rates are quoted: 4.00% for 30 days and 4.20% for 90 days, both on a simple basis. Derive the forward repo rate for days 30 to 90, and compute it.
back:
Step 1: no-arbitrage requires that lending for 90 days equals lending for 30 days then rolling at the forward rate \(f\) for 60 days.
Step 2: \((1+r_2 t_2)=(1+r_1 t_1)\,(1+f\,(t_2-t_1))\), with \(t_1=30/365\), \(t_2=90/365\).
Step 3: solve \(f=\dfrac{1}{t_2-t_1}\left[\dfrac{1+r_2t_2}{1+r_1t_1}-1\right]\).
Step 4: \(r_1 t_1=0.3288\%\), \(r_2 t_2=1.0356\%\). Ratio \(=1.010356/1.003288=1.007046\). Dividing \(0.7046\%\) by \(60/365=0.16438\) gives \(f\approx 4.29\%\).
Interpretation: the forward sits above the 90-day rate because the upward slope of the term curve is embedded in the spot-to-forward roll.
Where it breaks: this ignores the term premium and the bid-offer in term repo, and it assumes the same collateral basket is available in both legs.
Forward repo for days 30 to 90 implied by the 4.00% and 4.20% term rates: 4.29%.

front: Derivation: Buy a bond at dirty price \(P\) (per 100 face), finance it in repo at rate \(r\) for \(\tau\), and receive one coupon \(C\) at time \(t_c\) within the period. Derive the forward dirty price \(F\) and evaluate for \(P=100.50\), \(r=4\%\), \(\tau=0.50\), \(C=2.00\) at \(t_c=0.25\).
back:
Step 1: the cost of carrying the bond is the repo interest on the dirty price, \(P\,r\,\tau\), so the bond must be sold at \(P(1+r\tau)\) to break even.
Step 2: the coupon received at \(t_c\) is reinvested at the repo rate to the forward date \(T\), so its future value is \(C\,(1+r(T-t_c))\). Subtract it from the required sale price.
Step 3: \(F = P(1+r\tau)-C\,(1+r(T-t_c))\).
Step 4: numerically \(F=100.50\times 1.02-2.00\times 1.01=102.51-2.02=100.49\).
Clean forward price is \(F\) minus accrued interest at \(T\). Note that the forward is on dirty price, which is what the repo sees.
Where it breaks: the coupon reinvestment rate should be the rate actually earned on cash, not necessarily the repo rate; under specialness the financing rate on the bond differs from the reinvestment rate.

front: Derivation: Derive the carry of a long bond financed in repo over a period \(\tau\), assuming the clean price is unchanged. Use position \(N\), coupon \(c\), dirty price \(P_d\) (per 100 face) and repo rate \(r\). Evaluate for \(N=£100\text{m}\), \(c=4.00\%\), \(P_d=100\), \(r=3.50\%\), \(\tau=0.25\).
back:
Step 1: coupon accrual over \(\tau\) is \(N\,c\,\tau\), since accrued interest rises linearly with time.
Step 2: with clean price constant, the dirty price rises only through accrued interest, so there is no capital gain other than accrual.
Step 3: repo cost is \(r\,\tau\) times the cash borrowed, which is \(N\,P_d/100\).
Step 4: carry \(=N\,\tau\left(c-r\,\dfrac{P_d}{100}\right)\). For the numbers: \(100\text{m}\times0.25\times(0.04-0.035\times1.00)=£125{,}000\).
Where it breaks: (a) a special bond's financing rate is below the GC rate, so the carry is larger than this formula gives; (b) day-count mismatch between semi-annual Act/Act coupons and Act/365 repo; (c) on the coupon date the clean price drops, so carry must be computed on dirty prices across the coupon.
Carry on GBP 100m: coupon accrual GBP 1.000m less repo cost GBP 0.875m = GBP 125,000.

front: Derivation: A dealer holds bond market value \(MV\) funded with haircut \(h\), with the remaining \(h\cdot MV\) funded by equity at cost \(r_e\). Derive the effective financing rate per unit of MV and the return on equity. Evaluate for yield \(y=5\%\), repo \(R=4\%\), \(h=2\%\), \(r_e=5.5\%\).
back:
Step 1: cash borrowed in repo is \((1-h)\,MV\), at rate \(R\).
Step 2: equity funds \(h\,MV\), at cost \(r_e\).
Step 3: effective financing cost per unit MV is \(R_{eff}=(1-h)R+h\,r_e\).
Step 4: net carry per unit MV after charging equity at \(r_e\) is \(y-R_{eff}\). Accounting ROE, before charging the cost of equity, is \(\dfrac{y-(1-h)R}{h}\). Economic return after charging equity is \(\dfrac{y-R_{eff}}{h}\).
Numbers: \(R_{eff}=0.98\times4\%+0.02\times5.5\%=4.03\%\). Net carry after equity \(=0.97\%\). Accounting ROE \(=(5\%-3.92\%)/2\%=54\%\). Economic return after equity cost \(=0.97\%/2\%=48.5\%\).
So charging equity at 5.5% lowers the return by about 5.5 points here, from 54% to 48.5%.
Where it breaks: ROE is very sensitive to \(h\) because it divides by \(h\). Halving the haircut doubles the leverage and roughly doubles the spread's contribution, which is why haircut moves drive desk limits.

front: Derivation: Derive the compounded-in-arrears SONIA coupon over a period with daily rates \(r_i\) and day counts \(d_i\) (Act/365). Evaluate for 4.00% over 3 days (Friday to Monday), 4.00% for 1 day, and 4.10% for 3 days.
back:
Step 1: a unit of cash grows by \(\prod_i (1+r_i d_i/365)\) over the period.
Step 2: the period's annualised compounded rate is \(R = \dfrac{365}{D}\left[\prod_i (1+r_i d_i/365)-1\right]\), where \(D=\sum d_i\).
Step 3: here \(D=7\). The rates are 4.00% for 3 days, 4.00% for 1 day and 4.10% for 3 days, so the product is \((1+0.04\cdot3/365)(1+0.04/365)(1+0.041\cdot3/365)\), which gives \(\approx 1.000776\) over the period, and the annualised compounded rate is \(\approx 4.044\%\).
Step 4: the day-weighted simple average is \((4.00\cdot3+4.00\cdot1+4.10\cdot3)/7=4.043\%\). The compounded figure sits marginally above it because the higher rate is applied to a grown balance.
Where it breaks: the observation shift or lookback changes which \(r_i\) are used, and the rate for the last days is not known until the period ends, so pricing uses a projected curve for those days.

front: Derivation: Derive the breakeven TRS spread over SOFR at which a total return swap (TRS) funds the bond at the same all-in cost as repo with haircut \(h\), repo spread \(b\) over SOFR, and equity cost \(r_e\). Evaluate for \(h=2\%\), \(b=15\)bp, \(r_e=5.5\%\), SOFR \(=4.00\%\).
back:
Step 1: repo effective financing per unit exposure is \((1-h)(S+b)+h\,r_e\), where \(S\) is SOFR.
Step 2: the TRS funding leg pays SOFR plus spread \(s\) on the full notional. There is no cash borrowed and no haircut, so no equity term appears on the TRS side.
Step 3: equate the two: \(S+s=(1-h)(S+b)+h\,r_e\), giving \(s^*=(1-h)\,b+h\,(r_e-S)\).
Step 4: \(s^*=0.98\times15+0.02\times(5.5\%-4.0\%)=14.7+3.0=17.7\)bp.
Where it breaks: this excludes capital and leverage charges on the swap versus repo, counterparty margin on the TRS, and the fact that a TRS can give off-balance-sheet exposure that the leverage ratio treats differently.

front: Derivation: Derive the first-order sensitivity of carry to the repo rate, and express it as a repo DV01 for a £100m position held for one year.
back:
Step 1: carry \(=N\,\tau\,(c-r\,P_d/100)\) from the previous derivation. Differentiate with respect to \(r\): \(\partial\text{carry}/\partial r=-N\,\tau\,P_d/100\).
Step 2: for \(P_d=100\) and \(\tau=1\) year, a 1bp move in \(r\) changes carry by \(100\text{m}\times0.0001\times1=£10{,}000\) per year.
Step 3: this is the repo DV01 of the funding leg. It is linear in \(N\) and in \(\tau\), and it does not depend on the coupon.
Where it breaks: the sensitivity is to the marginal repo rate paid, not to the GC rate. A special bond's sensitivity is to its special rate, and a haircut change moves the cash borrowed, so it adds a second sensitivity of \(\partial\text{cash}/\partial h=-N\).

front: Derivation: Derive the lender's net revenue from a securities loan where cash collateral is reinvested at \(r_{reinv}\) and the borrower earns rebate \(r_{reb}\). Use securities value \(V\), 102% collateral, and evaluate for \(V=£20\text{m}\), \(r_{reinv}=4.00\%\), \(r_{reb}=3.25\%\) for 30 days.
back:
Step 1: cash collateral \(=1.02\,V\).
Step 2: the lender reinvests the cash at \(r_{reinv}\) and pays the borrower the rebate \(r_{reb}\) on the same cash.
Step 3: spread revenue \(=1.02\,V\,(r_{reinv}-r_{reb})\,\tau\), plus any separately negotiated lending fee.
Step 4: \(20.4\text{m}\times0.0075\times30/365=£12{,}575\).
Where it breaks: the spread term is positive only while the rebate is below the reinvestment rate. In a special security the rebate is low and the lender earns more; in a general security the rebate sits close to reinvestment and the lender relies on the lending fee.

front: Case study: Special repo value to a bondholder. A £10m holding of a gilt is special at 3.20% against 4.00% GC. Compute the value of specialness over 30 days and state the annualised equivalent.
back:
Step 1: specialness \(=4.00\%-3.20\%=0.80\%\), annualised.
Step 2: value over 30 days \(=10{,}000{,}000\times0.0080\times30/365=£6{,}575\).
Step 3: annualised equivalent is 80bp on £10m, or £80,000 per year if the bond stays special.
Sanity check: 30 days is about a twelfth of a year, so \(80{,}000/12\approx6{,}667\), close to \(6{,}575\) once Act/365 is applied to a 30-day period.
Interviewer follow-up: why is this not the whole value? The holder also earns the lending fee in some structures and can cover a short without selling, so the true value includes the availability option.

front: Case study: Basis trade financing breakeven. A fund holds £100m of the CTD, shorts the future, and finances the cash bond at 4.00% repo with a 2% haircut. The implied repo from the futures is 4.30%. Over 90 days, compute the excess carry, the return on the fund's equity, and the repo rate at which the trade breaks even.
back:
Step 1: excess carry \(=£100\text{m}\times(4.30\%-4.00\%)\times90/360=£75{,}000\).
Step 2: equity \(=2\%\times£100\text{m}=£2\text{m}\). This is a simplification: the full £100m is treated as earning the 30bp excess, and the 98m cash financing is not costed separately. Return on equity over 90 days \(=75{,}000/2{,}000{,}000=3.75\%\), which annualises to about \(3.75\%\times365/90\approx15.2\%\).
Step 3: breakeven repo rate is the implied repo of 4.30%, since at that rate excess carry is zero. A 30bp rise in repo eliminates the carry.
Step 4: a 2% haircut magnifies this: the same 30bp of spread is a 15% return on equity, which is why haircut levels and funding stability matter as much as the basis itself.
Interviewer follow-up: what does this sum ignore? Equity cost, margin for variation on the futures, and the change in the CTD's implied repo as the basis moves.

front: Case study: Year-end turn cost. A dealer funds a £1bn book in GC repo. For a 3-day year-end window, GC spikes by 250bp to 6.50%, against a normal 4.00%. Compute the extra financing cost, then compare it with the book's daily carry if the bonds yield 4.50% against 4.00% funding.
back:
Step 1: extra cost \(=£1\text{bn}\times2.50\%\times3/365=£205{,}479\).
Step 2: book carry per day at a 50bp positive spread \(=£1\text{bn}\times0.005/365=£13{,}699\).
Step 3: the turn cost equals about \(205{,}479/13{,}699\approx15\) days of normal carry.
Step 4: the spike comes from window dressing, since banks shrink gross repo on reporting dates to reduce leverage-ratio exposure. It is a funding cost that an unhedged overnight book pays, and a term repo or a term-out across the reporting date removes it.
Sanity check: the turn cost is about 4.1% of the annual carry on the £5m-per-year book, so it is material but not decisive. It is worth paying for a term-out only if the spike is larger or the book is larger.
Interviewer follow-up: how would you hedge the turn? Term out the book across the reporting date with a term repo or an interest-rate swap on funding, and accept the term premium.

front: Case study: TRS vs repo cost comparison. Exposure of $100m of a bond for one year, SOFR at 4.00%. Repo is at SOFR + 15bp with a 2% haircut and equity costs 5.5%. The TRS is at SOFR + 75bp with no haircut. Compare all-in annual costs and find the breakeven TRS spread.
back:
Step 1: repo effective rate per unit exposure \(=(1-h)(S+b)+h\,r_e=0.98\times4.15\%+0.02\times5.5\%=4.177\%\).
Step 2: repo cost on $100m for one year \(=\$4.177\text{m}\).
Step 3: TRS cost \(=100\text{m}\times(4.00\%+0.75\%)=\$4.75\text{m}\).
Step 4: the TRS costs \(\$0.573\)m more per year, i.e. about 57bp of exposure. Breakeven TRS spread is \(17.7\)bp over SOFR, from the derivation.
Sanity check: the TRS spread exceeds the repo spread by 60bp (75 minus 15), but the repo effective spread is 17.7bp, not 15bp, because of the 3bp equity term. The net gap is 75 minus 17.7, about 57.3bp, which matches the $0.573m difference.
Interviewer follow-up: when would a rational desk still pay the TRS? When it saves balance-sheet or leverage charges, when the repo cannot be executed for the collateral, or when the TRS avoids the regulatory cost of gross repo exposure that the leverage ratio counts.
Annual cost on $100m: repo $4.177m vs TRS $4.75m, TRS dearer by $0.573m.

front: Case study: Haircut stress on ROE. A dealer holds £100m of a bond yielding 5.00%, funded at 4.00% repo, with equity fixed at £2m and no outside capital. Haircut rises from 2% to 10%. Compute the position the desk can hold, the forced sale, and the ROE before and after.
back:
Step 1: at 2%, equity \(=2\) supports \(2/0.02=£100\text{m}\). Carry \(=100\times(5.00\%-0.98\times4.00\%)=£1.08\)m per year, ROE \(=54\%\) on £2m.
Step 2: at 10%, equity \(=2\) supports \(2/0.10=£20\text{m}\). The desk must sell \(£80\text{m}\) to meet the haircut.
Step 3: if the desk instead keeps £100m, it needs £10m equity, an £8m shortfall.
Step 4: ROE if it shrinks to £20m (same funding structure): carry \(=20\times(5.00\%-0.90\times4.00\%)=£0.28\)m on £2m, ROE \(=14\%\). The ROE falls by 40 points, and the desk is also forced into a sale at the stressed price.
Interviewer follow-up: how would you pre-empt this? Hold an extra equity buffer proportional to the stressed haircut, and limit the position to what survives a 10% haircut shock.
Haircut stress: position GBP 100m to GBP 20m on GBP 2m equity; ROE 54% to 14%.

front: Case study: Repo-OIS basis cost. A dealer funds £500m overnight at GC repo of 4.10% while SONIA-based OIS is 4.00%. Compute the annual cost of the 10bp basis and the cost over 30 days.
back:
Step 1: basis \(=4.10\%-4.00\%=10\)bp per year.
Step 2: annual cost \(=£500\text{m}\times0.0010=£500{,}000\).
Step 3: 30-day cost \(=500\text{m}\times0.0010\times30/365=£41{,}096\).
Step 4: sanity check against a 10bp per year move: the basis cost per bp of £500m for a year is £50,000, so 10bp is £500,000.
Interviewer follow-up: is a positive repo-OIS basis a cost for a dealer or a signal? Both. It is a cost to funding the book and a signal of collateral scarcity or balance-sheet constraint, and the desk should separate the two using the term structure of the basis.

front: Case study: Negative repo cost on a special. A dealer is short €100m of a bond that trades at a -0.50% (Act/360) overnight special repo rate. It borrows the bond by lending cash through reverse repo and keeps the position open for 14 calendar days. Compute the amount the dealer pays.
back:
Step 1: with a negative rate, the repurchase price is below the purchase price, so the cash lender (here the dealer) pays the other side.
Step 2: the dealer's cash lent is the reverse-repo leg. Interest \(=\text{Notional}\times r\times d/360=100\text{m}\times(-0.005)\times14/360=-€19{,}444\), so the dealer pays about €19.4k over 14 days.
Step 3: the per-day cost is about €1,389, which matches the one-day repurchase arithmetic in the specialness chain.
Step 4: the position is only worth holding if the short is needed to hedge or deliver; the negative special is the price of that flexibility.
Step 5: the price of owning this collateral is the negative repo rate, so the desk should only accept it when the position is needed for a hedge or a delivery.
Interviewer follow-up: why does the desk not just deposit cash at the central bank? If the deposit rate is also negative, the comparison is the depth of the deposit rate versus the special rate, which is the constraint that limits how negative specials can go.

front: Case study: Fails charge on a special bond. A dealer fails to deliver $100m of a bond for 2 days, with a 1.50% reference rate and a fails charge set at max(3% less reference, 0) (TMPG-style, approx.). Compute the charge paid, and the reference rate at which the charge is zero.
back:
Step 1: charge rate \(=\max(3\%-r_{ref},0)=\max(3\%-1.50\%,0)=1.50\%\) per annum.
Step 2: charge \(=100\text{m}\times0.015\times2/360=\$8{,}333\).
Step 3: the charge is zero at a reference rate of 3% or above. At a reference rate of 4.50%, as in the earlier draft, the charge would be zero.
Step 4: sanity check: 1.50% for 2 days on $100m is about 0.8bp of notional.
Interviewer follow-up: why do fails persist when the charge is zero? The buyer still loses its hedge and carry, so the total cost of a fail is not the fails charge alone.

front: Case study: Securities lending revenue. A lender loans £20m of gilts for 30 days, takes cash collateral of 102%, reinvests at 4.00% and pays a 3.25% rebate. Compute the spread revenue and say how it changes if the bond goes special.
back:
Step 1: cash collateral \(=20\text{m}\times1.02=£20.4\text{m}\).
Step 2: spread \(=4.00\%-3.25\%=0.75\%\).
Step 3: revenue \(=20.4\text{m}\times0.0075\times30/365=£12{,}575\).
Step 4: if the bond goes special, the rebate falls (the borrower pays less to borrow cash), so the spread rises and the lender earns more. If it becomes general collateral, the rebate rises toward reinvestment and the spread compresses.
Interviewer follow-up: what is the lender's main risk? Reinvestment risk on the cash and a run if the collateral is sold, which is why cash collateral reinvestment is a credit exposure.

front: Why does a dealer sometimes find that its repo-OIS spread is positive while its leverage ratio is slack, and what does that tell you about the source of the basis?
back:
Headline: a positive repo-OIS spread with slack leverage means the cost is set by collateral scarcity or intermediation capacity, not by balance-sheet cost on gross exposures.
If leverage is slack, the marginal constraint is elsewhere, such as the LCR (which rewards holding HQLA) or the balance-sheet cost of unsecured funding. A positive basis then reflects demand for specific collateral.
Interviewer follow-up: how would you tell collateral scarcity from balance-sheet cost? Scarcity shows up in specials and in the term structure of the basis, while balance-sheet cost shows up in quarter-end and year-end spikes that reverse.

front: Explain why a leveraged basis trade is financed through repo, and name the three risks that can unwind it.
back:
Headline: the cash bond is financed in repo, which is cheap and secured, and the futures leg needs margin but no principal funding. The trade earns the excess of implied repo over actual financing.
The three unwind risks: (1) haircut increases, which force a sale of bonds (see the stress case); (2) the repo rate rises or the CTD switches, which compresses the basis; (3) margin calls on the futures leg, which require liquid cash at the worst time.
Interviewer follow-up: which is most dangerous? Haircut and margin calls together, because they are procyclical and hit at the same time as the basis widens.

front: Under Basel's NSFR, how is a reverse repo of Level 1 collateral against a financial counterparty with under six months to maturity treated, and why does that matter for a dealer's funding plan?
back:
Headline: Basel's NSFR (standard para. 38) assigns a 10% required stable funding factor to a reverse repo with a financial counterparty, with residual maturity under six months, secured by Level 1 assets.
Some jurisdictions have applied a lower factor: the EU CRR has applied 0% to some Level 1 short-term reverse repos, and alignment with the Basel factor has been under discussion. Check the current text applicable to the desk.
Why it matters: secured lending against Level 1 collateral needs less stable funding than unsecured lending, so it supports the NSFR relative to unsecured lending, but under the Basel factor it still requires some stable funding.
Interviewer follow-up: what is the trade-off? Short-maturity secured lending helps the ratio but increases roll-over and rate risk, which the NSFR does not fully capture.

front: Secured versus unsecured funding: why is the desk's secured funding cheaper, and what drives the secured-unsecured basis?
back:
Headline: secured funding is cheaper because the lender holds collateral and has priority in default, so it accepts a lower rate. The desk pays for the difference through its haircut and collateral cost.
The secured-unsecured basis is the spread between unsecured term funding and secured repo, and it widens when collateral is scarce, when unsecured credit is priced higher, or when secured funding is concentrated in a few counterparties.
Interviewer follow-up: how does FTP reflect this? The funds transfer price charges each business line the marginal secured cost for assets that can be pledged, and the unsecured term spread for the rest.

front: The Fed's {{c1::ON RRP}} rate sits at the {{c2::bottom}} of the target range and the Standing Repo Facility rate sits at the {{c3::top}}, forming a corridor for SOFR.
back: Interest on reserves sits inside the range. The corridor bounds repo rates in both ample and scarce reserve regimes.

front: Under the Basel LCR, Level 1 assets carry a {{c1::0%}} haircut and Level 2A assets carry a {{c2::15%}} haircut, approximately.
back: These are the standard LCR haircut levels for liquid assets when counted as HQLA; the calibration is an approximation, not a derivation.

front: Under SEC Rule {{c1::15c3-3}}, US broker-dealers may rehypothecate customer collateral up to {{c2::140%}} of customer debit balances.
back: The cap is the reason prime brokerage funding is limited by client debit balances, and it is a US rule that does not apply directly in the UK.

front: The UK leverage ratio minimum is {{c1::3.25%}} of exposure measure, and the US enhanced supplementary leverage buffer for G-SIB holding companies is set at {{c2::50%}} of the Method 1 GSIB surcharge, on top of the 3% minimum.
back: The UK ratio applies to firms in scope of the PRA thresholds. The 3.25% level replaced 3% in 2017 to offset the exclusion of central bank claims. The US final rule (November 2025, effective 1 April 2026, with early adoption from 1 January 2026) replaced the old 2% eSLR buffer, which made the holding-company requirement 5%, with a buffer equal to half the surcharge. Repo and reverse repo count largely at gross value in these ratios, which is why a leverage-constrained dealer shrinks gross repo rather than net.

front: Securities lending collateral is typically {{c1::102%}} of the loaned value for US domestic securities and {{c2::105%}} for international securities, which is a market convention (approximately).
back: The margin above 100% protects the lender against a move in the loaned security's value between margin calls.

front: A repo rate quoted at 4.00% on Act/360 is equivalent to about {{c1::4.06%}} on an Act/365 basis, because {{c2::365/360}} scales the periodic rate.
back: Same money, different denominator. Mixing bases on two legs of a swap or basis trade creates a spurious spread.

front: The reformed SONIA is a {{c1::trimmed-mean}} of {{c2::unsecured}} overnight sterling transactions, published by the {{c3::Bank of England}}.
back: The reformed SONIA replaced the earlier, thinner survey-based series; the transaction base is the reason it is more robust.
